store.2: The user's favorite class this semester is Advanced Algorithms. They find the theoretical aspects of problem-solving fascinating, particularly in optimizing pathfinding in large networks and handling huge datasets with minimal time complexity. The class covers dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems, which can be challenging but engaging. The professor is skilled at explaining complex concepts in an intuitive manner, making the material more accessible. The user leaves each class with a buzzing mind, eager to explore more.
store.3: The user is taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which they find to be the second most challenging. The course involves extensive reading, group discussions, and a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure, requiring collaboration with individuals having different coding styles and ideas about the final product. This diversity is beneficial as it prepares students for real-world scenarios where integration and handling of concurrency issues and node failures are crucial. The user experienced a nerve-wracking moment when troubleshooting a bug caused by a misplaced bracket in a config file, but the sense of accomplishment upon resolving it was immense.
store.4: The user is taking an elective in Game Design, which aligns with their major when combined with other specific classes. They have always been a gamer at heart, making this course a must-take. The professor is from the industry, having worked on indie games that received some attention. The course covers basic 2D and 3D engines, physics implementation, and user experience design. The assignments are highly creative, making the course enjoyable. The user recently designed a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, focusing on balancing the difficulty curve to prevent player frustration. It was challenging but rewarding to see the design come together.
store.5: The user initially found Introduction to Quantum Computing intimidating, but now they enjoy it. The professor's approach emphasizes conceptual understanding over pure math, making it more accessible. The course includes linear algebra, but it's balanced with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. They're not building actual quantum computers, but rather modeling algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to demonstrate their theoretical advantages over classical methods. This has expanded the user's perspective on problem-solving, making it mind-blowing.
store.6: The user's Capstone Project course is the sink-or-swim part of their senior year. They have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. The user and their group decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. They're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts based on tweets or posts that suggest a disaster or crisis. This project is pulling together everything the user has learned as a CS major, including database management, API building, front-end interface, and ML pipeline. They're also learning about project management and organization, with one team member serving as the Scrum Master and leading daily stand-ups and sprints. It's a lot to handle, but if they can successfully complete it, they'll be proud of their accomplishment.
store.7: The user is taking a humanities elective, Philosophy of Mind, which is their last required non-CS elective. They chose it because it ties into AI in interesting ways, exploring concepts like consciousness, the nature of mind, and its application to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, allowing for in-depth discussions, which is a welcome change from the coding-heavy nature of their other classes. It helps them analyze abstract ideas and consider the broader implications of building AI systems that could simulate human thinking. The user recently wrote a paper on whether strong AI could truly experience qualia, such as subjective experiences like color or pain. This topic is significant in the philosophy world, and they found the research fascinating. They believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is crucial, and this course provides valuable perspective.
store.8: The user's schedule is typical of a college student, with Mondays and Wednesdays being the most packed. Mondays start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before the Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, there's the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are lighter, with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be challenging if the user is tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but they're often filled with assignments, group projects, or labs. The user also dedicates time to undergrad research in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets, which adds to their workload. They're determined to push through and make the most of their senior year.
store.9: The user's biggest challenge this semester is balancing group projects. The Capstone project requires around ten hours per week, with more time needed if they encounter bugs or if the model doesn't train properly. The Distributed Systems project is another significant time commitment, with the group meeting at least twice a week. They use Slack or Discord to stay updated and coordinate their schedules, which can be a logistical challenge. Despite the stress, the user finds it exciting to have the opportunity to fully invest in academic projects without the pressures of a job environment. It's a chance to learn and explore without the added responsibilities of a professional setting.
store.10: The user is having a great time despite the challenges of their senior year. They've become more confident in their problem-solving and time management skills, which has reduced their anxiety about taking on tough CS classes. While they still experience late nights when faced with debugging or tight deadlines, they no longer find it as daunting as they did in the past. As a senior, they've developed resourcefulness, collaboration skills, and critical thinking abilities. They believe that these classes, although demanding, are highly rewarding and directly contribute to their future career. It's a great feeling to see their hard work paying off and knowing that they're building towards their desired career.
store.11: I have been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it has been one of the most eye-opening parts of my college experience. It has given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and it's fascinating to be a part of it. As a freshman, I didn't see myself going down the research route. I was into coding projects and hackathons, but I didn't think research was something that aligned with my interests. However, one of my professors, who taught an introductory data science class, noticed my ability to bridge technical coding with user experience. She informed me about an opening for a research assistant in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific datasets. I was initially hesitant because research seemed intimidating, but I decided to take the leap. It turned out to be a great decision.

store.14: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists collaborate with scientists from various backgrounds, such as astronomy, environmental science, and neuroscience, to make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. In classes, you might work with small datasets or 1GB datasets for machine learning projects. In our lab, we handle datasets that are tens of terabytes in size. Visualizing such data so that domain experts(like astrophysicists) can quickly extract insights is a significant challenge. One of my main tasks is developing front-end prototypes that present data slices in dynamic, interactive dashboards. This involves using advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering if we're dealing with 3D data.
store.15: The first research project I really got into was visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had daily temperature readings from buoys all around the Pacific, scattered across different servers. The raw data was enormous, consisting of tons of files, each representing a single day's worth of readings at tiny intervals. Our task was to aggregate and present the data in a coherent manner to show patterns over months or years. I dove in headfirst, writing scripts to clean and unify the data, building a pipeline that could handle near real-time updates, and designing interfaces that allowed researchers to zoom into specific regions or timeframes. Eventually, I co-authored my first paper on this system. It was surreal to see my name in an official publication, and it's probably one of my proudest moments in college.
store.16: These days, my research has pivoted to immersive analytics platforms. We're exploring how VR or AR technologies can help scientists gain a more intuitive understanding of complex data. Looking at raw numerical data in a spreadsheet is one thing, and 2D visuals like graphs are another step up. However, being able to walk around a 3D representation of data in a virtual environment, interact with it, rotate it, and highlight subsets is a game-changer. It's a significant leap from coding up websites. There's a lot of experimentation involved, such as plugging in VR headsets, integrating with engines like Unity or Unreal, and figuring out how to efficiently stream data into a 3D environment. It's all cutting-edge, which makes it exciting. Every day, you're forging your own path because there isn't a well-established best-practice library for VR data visualization yet.
store.17: Research life is not just about coding away in a quiet corner. It's a lot of reading, especially when you're trying to solve a specific problem, like rendering volumetric data in VR. It's likely that someone has attempted something similar and published their findings in a conference proceeding or workshop. I need to comb through those papers to see if they can provide any insights. It can be overwhelming, but over time, you learn how to skim effectively, focusing on the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to determine if a paper is relevant. Occasionally, when I find something interesting, I share it with the rest of the lab, and we discuss how we can incorporate that technique into our own workflow.
store.18: I also get to interact with a bunch of graduate students, both master's and PhD candidates. It can be intimidating at first because they're so deeply immersed in their niche fields, but it's also inspiring. There's a PhD student in our lab who's developing a machine learning algorithm for on-the-fly compression of large datasets and integrating it with our VR platform. The idea is that when looking at a huge climate dataset, you don't need to have every single point fully loaded at once in VR—a compressed representation might be enough until you zoom in. It's wild, but super practical for real-time performance. Working alongside him allows me to see how advanced theoretical concepts are applied in real-world scenarios. Some of our best brainstorming sessions happen spontaneously, like in the lab break room, sipping coffee and hashing out how we can offload processing to the GPU.
store.19: We've also done a few poster presentations at smaller symposiums around campus, which was a great experience. You have to distill complex research into easy-to-understand visuals and talking points. The first time I presented, I was nervous, but it turned out to be more like a friendly dialogue. People are genuinely interested in what you're doing. There were even a few folks from local startups who showed up, and they shared interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries, such as marketing analytics or architecture. It opened my eyes to how research can transition from academia to real-world applications.
store.20: I've been lucky enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and I'm currently working on a larger conference submission. The bigger conference is the IEEE Visualization Conference(IEEE VIS), which is a significant event in our field. We're focusing on a user study that compares traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. Our hypothesis is that VR immersion helps researchers spot anomalies or trends faster than they would with a plain 2D chart. We ran a small set of user trials with 15 participants, recorded their times, and asked them to fill out a UX questionnaire. Now we're crunching the data to see if there's a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a collaborative effort: I'm handling the sections on system architecture and prototype design, someone else is writing about the user study methodology, and our PI is weaving it all into a cohesive narrative. It's a balancing act, especially with my senior coursework and capstone project to manage.
store.21: I get asked if I plan on going to grad school. Right now, I'm considering working in the industry for a couple of years, hopefully at a tech company that values R&D or advanced solution building. This will help me decide if I want to pursue a master's or PhD later on. The idea of contributing to cutting-edge knowledge is tempting, especially in areas like data visualization or machine learning. However, I also want to see how these concepts are applied in real product development. One of my mentors in the lab suggested that working in industry can provide a better perspective on what problems are truly relevant, which will help me approach a PhD with a more practical mindset.
store.22: It's not all sunshine and rainbows. Research can be frustrating. You might spend weeks on an approach that doesn't pan out, or you might discover that your idea has already been done and improved upon by a group in Europe or somewhere else. That can be tough to swallow. However, the key is to adapt. We read that existing paper, incorporate their findings, think of a new angle or application, and push the boundaries. That's the essence of research. You're never truly starting from scratch; you're building on the foundation laid by others. The sense of collaboration within our lab and among the global research community is truly special.
store.23: One story that stands out was when one of our massive servers crashed a few months ago. We had vital data stored there, some of which wasn't fully backed up(I know, a rookie mistake, but we learned from it). I remember the scramble that night: a frantic email chain, Zoom calls with the lab manager, everyone trying to see if we could recover the data. We managed to restore most of it, but that crisis drove home the importance of data backups. After that, we set up a better backup system and implemented checks to ensure we wouldn't rely on a single point of failure again. It was stressful, but it also became a bonding experience for the whole lab.
store.24: Research has connected me with professors on a more personal level than just being a face in the lecture hall. My PI is super approachable; if I have a question about my career direction or something I'm struggling with in class, I know I can pop into her office and chat. She's been recommending me for different scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. I even got to attend a virtual workshop on immersive analytics filled with academic experts from around the world. Witnessing them debate technical details, propose new frameworks, and even gently tease each other over rival theories was fascinating. It was like I was witnessing the frontier of CS knowledge in real time.
store.25: That's basically my journey in the research world so far. It's a lot of work, often more chaotic than you'd expect, but also super rewarding. I love the feeling that what I do in the lab might shape the way scientists understand their data five or ten years down the line. Maybe one day the VR and immersive stuff we're trying to pioneer will become standard tools, and I'll be able to look back and say, 'Hey, I was part of that from the beginning.' It's that sense of contributing to something bigger that really keeps me motivated. Whether or not I go to grad school soon, I know this experience has changed how I think about computer science, innovation, and teamwork. I couldn't imagine my undergrad years without it—it's definitely enriched my perspective on what it means to be a computer scientist.
